title: Hecho vs Echo: The Silent H That Changes Everything

meta_description: Hecho vs echo: hecho comes from hacer (done, made, fact), echo comes from echar (I throw, I pour). Rules, expressions like echar de menos, mistakes and a quiz.
excerpt: Same sound, different verbs: why the silent h matters.

body_html:
Hecho vs echo is a classic spelling trap, because the h in Spanish is silent and both words sound exactly the same. But they come from different verbs. Hecho, with h, comes from hacer (to do, to make): He hecho la cena (I’ve made dinner). Echo, without h, comes from echar (to throw, put, pour): Echo sal a la sopa (I put salt in the soup). Know the verb, and you know the spelling.

Quick answer
  • Hecho = done, made (participle of hacer): ¿Qué has hecho?
  • Hecho = fact, event (noun): un hecho histórico.
  • Echo = I throw, pour, put (from echar): Te echo de menos.
  • Test: if you can say hacer, it’s hecho; if echar, it’s echo.
{{toc}}

Hecho vs echo: the core rule

HechoEcho
Comes fromhacer (to do, make)echar (to throw, put, pour)
FormPast participle; nounFirst person present: I throw
ExampleLo he hecho yo. I made it.Echo la carta al buzón. I mail the letter.

The RAE dictionary lists dozens of meanings for echar, from throwing and pouring to firing someone and starting to do something.

Hecho: done, made, fact

As a participle of hacer

  • ¿Has hecho los deberes? Have you done your homework?
  • Hemos hecho una tarta. We’ve made a cake.
  • Hecho a mano. Handmade.
  • Un trabajo bien hecho. A job well done.

As a noun: fact, event

  • Es un hecho. It’s a fact.
  • De hecho, ya lo sabía. In fact, I already knew.
  • Los hechos ocurrieron en 1998. The events took place in 1998.

Expressions

¡Hecho! (Deal!), Dicho y hecho (No sooner said than done), un hombre hecho y derecho (a grown man).

{{image:2}}

Echo: from echar

  • Echo azúcar al café. I put sugar in my coffee.
  • Siempre echo la siesta. I always take a nap.
  • Echo un vistazo. I take a look.
  • Te echo una mano. I’ll give you a hand.

Echar de menos

The most romantic use of all: Te echo de menos means “I miss you” in Spain (Latin America prefers Te extraño). Writing Te hecho de menos is one of the most common spelling mistakes in love messages! See {{link:long-distance-relationship-spanish|long-distance relationship messages in Spanish}}.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Other forms of echar

The same h-less spelling runs through the whole verb: echas, echa, echamos, echan; past eché, echó; participle echado. So Me han echado del trabajo (I’ve been fired), never hechado. And hacer keeps its h: hago, hice, hecho.

Why this is tricky for learners

Learners already know silent letters, but in Spanish the h is always silent, so the ear gives no clue at all. And because he hecho and echo can appear in similar contexts (He hecho la sopa / Le echo sal a la sopa), it is easy to grab the wrong one. The English word “echo” adds to the confusion; in Spanish, that sound repeating is eco, with no h and no ch.

A quick mental shortcut

Ask which infinitive you are thinking of. Could you rephrase with hacer (do, make)? Then write hecho. With echar (throw, put, pour, take a nap, give a hand, miss)? Then write echo. And if it means “fact”, it is always hecho.

More everyday expressions with echar

  • echar la culpa: to blame. Siempre me echa la culpa.
  • echar a perder: to ruin or spoil. La lluvia echó a perder el picnic.
  • echarse a reír / llorar: to burst out laughing / crying.
  • echar gasolina: to fill up with gas.
  • echar una película: to show a movie on TV (Spain). ¿Qué echan esta noche?

Every one of these is written without h, because they all come from echar. Once you see how many expressions use this verb, it becomes much easier to recognize when a sentence needs echo rather than hecho.

And with hacer: Lo hecho, hecho está means “What’s done is done”, a handy phrase for moving on after a mistake.

{{image:3}}

Try it yourself

  1. I miss my family. (Echo de menos a mi familia.)
  2. What have you done? (¿Qué has hecho?)
  3. In fact, it’s true. (De hecho, es verdad.)
  4. Shall I give you a hand? (¿Te echo una mano?)
  5. It’s homemade. (Está hecho en casa.)

Another silent-h pair: {{link:haber-vs-a-ver|haber vs a ver}}. All pairs in {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

With h: hecho, from hacer, or a fact. Without h: echo, from echar. And next time you write a love message, make sure it says Te echo de menos.

faq.q: What is the difference between hecho and echo?
faq.a: Hecho (with h) is the past participle of hacer (done, made) or a noun meaning fact. Echo (without h) is the present tense of echar: I throw, put or pour.

faq.q: Is it te echo de menos or te hecho de menos?
faq.a: Te echo de menos. It comes from the verb echar (echar de menos = to miss).

faq.q: How do you write “in fact” in Spanish?
faq.a: De hecho, with h, because hecho here is a noun meaning fact.
